chapter: Electric Charges, Fields and Gauss's Law
trick: Gauss's law only helps when the symmetry lets you pull E out of the integral — sphere, infinite line, infinite sheet. And note how the distance dependence changes: a point charge gives 1/r², an infinite line gives 1/r, an infinite sheet gives nothing at all. That progression is worth memorising as a set.

video.query: gauss law electric field due to line sheet sphere class 12 physics

data.prompt: Choose the field expression that applies to each charge distribution.

items.ask: Field at distance r from a point charge q
items.why: Coulomb's law through a spherical Gaussian surface of area 4πr² gives the inverse square.

items.ask: Field at distance r from an infinitely long line of charge, linear density λ
items.why: The Gaussian surface is a cylinder of area 2πrl, so one power of r survives — the field falls as 1/r, not 1/r².

items.ask: Field near an infinite plane sheet of surface density σ
items.why: Flux leaves through both flat faces, so the area is 2A and r cancels entirely — the field does not depend on distance.

items.ask: Field inside a uniformly charged conducting shell
items.why: A Gaussian surface inside encloses no charge, so the flux and hence the field are zero everywhere inside.

trick: Potential is a scalar and field is a vector, so potentials add arithmetically while fields add head-to-tail — at the midpoint of a dipole the field is large but the potential is zero. For capacitors, series and parallel are the reverse of resistors: capacitors in parallel simply add.

video.query: electrostatic potential capacitance series parallel combination class 12 physics

data.prompt: Work through a capacitor network step by step.
data.problem: Two capacitors of 3 μF and 6 μF are joined in series, and this combination is connected in parallel with a 4 μF capacitor. The whole network is across a 10 V supply.

steps.ask: What is the equivalent capacitance of the series pair?
steps.why: 1/C = 1/3 + 1/6 = 1/2, so C = 2 μF. In series the equivalent is always smaller than the smallest.

steps.ask: What is the total capacitance of the network?
steps.why: Capacitors in parallel add directly: 2 + 4 = 6 μF.

steps.ask: What total charge is drawn from the 10 V supply?
What energy is stored in the network?

data.answer: Series pair 2 μF, network 6 μF, charge 60 μC, energy 300 μJ.

chapter: Current Electricity: Ohm's Law, Kirchhoff and Wheatstone Bridge
trick: An AMMETER measures current, goes in SERIES, and must have very LOW resistance. A VOLTMETER measures potential difference, goes in PARALLEL, and must have very HIGH resistance. Every part of each sentence follows from the first word, and swapping the two is the single most common error on this chapter — an ammeter placed in parallel is a short circuit.

trick: A magnetic force never does work, because F = qv × B is always perpendicular to v — so a charged particle in a magnetic field changes direction but never speed. That is why the path is a circle and why kinetic energy is unchanged, and it disposes of a whole family of questions in one line.

video.query: biot savart law ampere circuital law force on moving charge class 12 physics

data.prompt: True or false? Mark each statement about magnetic fields and moving charges.

items.statement: A magnetic field can change the speed of a charged particle.
items.why: The force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work and the speed is constant. Only the direction changes.

items.statement: A charge moving parallel to a magnetic field feels no force.
items.why: F = qvB sin θ, and sin 0° = 0. The force is maximum when the motion is perpendicular to the field.

items.statement: The radius of the circular path is r = mv/qB.
items.why: Setting qvB equal to the centripetal force mv²/r and cancelling one v gives it.

items.statement: The time period of the circular motion depends on the particle's speed.
items.why: T = 2πm/qB — speed cancels out. This independence is what makes the cyclotron work.

items.statement: Two parallel wires carrying current in the same direction attract each other.
items.why: Same direction attracts, opposite repels — the definition of the ampere rests on this force.

items.statement: Ampere's circuital law relates the field around a closed loop to the current it encloses.
items.why: ∮B·dl = μ₀I, the magnetic counterpart of Gauss's law, and the quickest route to the field of a solenoid.

trick: Three magnetic materials, and susceptibility sorts them instantly: diamagnetic is small and negative, paramagnetic small and positive, ferromagnetic large and positive. Diamagnetics are repelled by a magnet and have no unpaired electrons — that last fact links this chapter straight back to chemistry.

trick: Lenz's law is conservation of energy wearing a disguise: the induced current always opposes the change that made it, because if it helped, you would get energy from nothing. Faraday gives the size of the emf, Lenz gives the minus sign — and it is the minus sign that questions test.

video.query: faraday law lenz law self and mutual inductance class 12 physics

data.prompt: True or false? Mark each statement about electromagnetic induction.

items.statement: An emf is induced only when the magnetic flux through the circuit changes.
items.why: A steady field, however strong, induces nothing. It is the rate of change of flux that matters.

items.statement: The minus sign in Faraday's law expresses conservation of energy.
items.why: It is Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the change. If it assisted, the current would grow without any work being done.

items.statement: Pushing a magnet north-pole-first into a coil makes the near face of the coil a north pole.
items.why: The coil opposes the approach by repelling the magnet, so it presents a like pole.

items.statement: Self-inductance depends on the current flowing through the coil.
items.why: It depends only on the geometry of the coil and the core material. Current determines the flux, not the inductance.

items.statement: Eddy currents are put to use in induction furnaces and electromagnetic braking.
items.why: They are a loss in a transformer core but a working principle in a brake — which is why cores are laminated but brake discs are not.

trick: A transformer steps voltage up and current down, or the reverse — power is conserved, so one goes up only if the other comes down. It works on alternating current alone, because direct current produces no changing flux. And a transformer cannot change frequency, whatever the turns ratio.

video.query: transformer step up step down turns ratio ac circuits class 12 physics

data.problem: An ideal transformer has 100 turns in the primary and 500 in the secondary. The primary is connected to a 220 V, 50 Hz supply and draws 5 A.

steps.ask: Is this a step-up or a step-down transformer?
steps.why: The secondary has more turns than the primary, so the voltage is raised.

steps.ask: What current flows in the secondary?
steps.why: Power is conserved in an ideal transformer: 220 × 5 = 1100 × Is, so Is = 1 A. Voltage up means current down.

steps.ask: What is the frequency of the secondary output?
steps.why: A transformer never changes frequency. The secondary follows the primary at 50 Hz.

data.answer: Step-up: 1100 V, 1 A, still 50 Hz. Power in equals power out at 1100 W.

trick: Order the spectrum by wavelength and you have half the chapter: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma — longest to shortest, and therefore lowest to highest energy. All of them travel at the same speed in vacuum, which is the fact questions try hardest to unsettle.

data.prompt: Arrange the electromagnetic spectrum from the longest wavelength to the shortest.

items.label: Radio waves
items.note: Broadcasting and communication; produced by oscillating circuits

items.label: Microwaves
items.note: Radar and microwave ovens; klystron and magnetron sources

items.label: Infrared
items.note: Heat radiation; produced by molecular vibration

items.label: Visible light
items.note: The narrow band the eye detects, about 400 to 700 nm

items.label: Ultraviolet
items.note: Absorbed by the ozone layer; causes sunburn and is used to sterilise

items.label: X-rays
items.note: Produced by fast electrons striking a metal target; medical imaging

items.label: Gamma rays
items.note: Shortest wavelength, highest energy; nuclear origin
